---
title: "Getting started"
description: "From a genotype matrix to a training set and a training set size."
---

```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 5, fig.height = 3.6, dpi = 120)
library(TSDFGS)
```

TSDFGS answers two questions before you phenotype anything:

1. **Which individuals** of a genotyped panel should be phenotyped as the training set?
2. **How many** are enough?

The input is a numeric matrix with one row per individual. Principal components (PCs) of the genotypes work well and keep the computation small; marker genotypes coded as -1, 0, 1 also work.

## The example data

`geno` holds the PCs of 404 rice accessions (Zhao et al., 2011), and `subpop` their sub-population. We keep the first 15 PCs of the first 150 accessions so that the examples run in seconds.

```{r data}
data(geno)
data(subpop)
g <- as.matrix(geno)[1:150, 1:15]
sp <- as.character(subpop)[1:150]
table(sp)
```

## Score a training set

A criterion compares a training set (`X`) with the test set (`X0`) whose breeding values you want to predict.

```{r score}
train <- 1:30
test <- 101:150
r_score(g[train, ], g[test, ])    # larger is better
cd_score(g[train, ], g[test, ])   # larger is better
pev_score(g[train, ], g[test, ])  # smaller is better
```

## Find a training set

`optTrain()` searches the candidates for the set with the best criterion. With a test set the search is *targeted*. Without one, the candidates that are not chosen act as the test set (*untargeted*).

```{r opt}
set.seed(1)
fit <- optTrain(g, cand = 1:100, n.train = 30, test = 101:150,
                method = "rScore", min.iter = 400, console = FALSE)
fit$OPTtrain              # rows of g to phenotype
fit$converged             # did the search stop by the convergence rule?
```

The criterion rises during the search and flattens when it has converged. Always look at it:

```{r trace, fig.alt = "Best r-score against iteration, rising and then flat."}
plot(fit$TOPscore, type = "l", col = "#0072B2", lwd = 2,
     xlab = "Iteration", ylab = "Best r-score so far")
```

A random set of the same size is the baseline to beat:

```{r random}
set.seed(2)
random_scores <- replicate(200, {
  s <- sample(1:100, 30)
  r_score(g[s, ], g[101:150, ])
})
c(optimized = r_score(g[fit$OPTtrain, ], g[101:150, ]),
  random_mean = mean(random_scores), random_max = max(random_scores))
```

### Sub-populations

If the panel has structure, pass `subpop` to keep every group represented in proportion. With a test set, `subpop` has one entry per row of `geno`.

```{r pop}
set.seed(1)
fit_pop <- optTrain(g, cand = 1:100, n.train = 30, test = 101:150, subpop = sp,
                    method = "rScore", min.iter = 400, console = FALSE)
table(sp[fit_pop$OPTtrain])
```

### Reproducible results

Pass `seed` to make a search reproducible. The same seed returns the same training set on any machine.

```{r seed}
a <- optTrain(g, 1:100, 30, min.iter = 400, console = FALSE, seed = 7)
b <- optTrain(g, 1:100, 30, min.iter = 400, console = FALSE, seed = 7)
identical(a$OPTtrain, b$OPTtrain)
```

## How many individuals?

`SSDFGS()` simulates the r-score for several training set sizes, fits a logistic growth curve, and returns the operating curve: the relative efficiency of the r-score (RErs) against the size. It is the slow step; use `multi.threads = TRUE` on Linux or macOS.

```{r ssdfgs, eval = FALSE}
res <- SSDFGS(geno)
res$OC.fig      # operating curve (needs ggplot2)
res$parameter   # alpha, beta, gamma of the growth curve
```

Read the size where RErs reaches 0.95 or 0.99 from the curve; it marks the point where more phenotyping adds little.
